Chapter Two: The Original Position and the Veil of Ignorance—Designing Fair Principles
Let’s dive into a fascinating thought experiment that helps us imagine what a truly fair society might look like.
Picture this—you’re in a group with a handful of other rational people, and together, you’ve got the incredible job of picking the basic rules that everyone in your society will live by. Sounds like a lot of pressure, right? But here’s the twist: you don’t know anything about your own life in this society. You have no clue about your social status, your talents, or even your personal values. You might end up rich, poor, healthy, sick, well-educated, or not at all.
This setup is called the original position. And that lack of personal info? That’s what we call the veil of ignorance.
It’s a clever way to make sure the rules you choose are really fair. If nobody knows where they’ll land—in the penthouse or the basement—there’s no reason to make rules that just benefit one group and hurt another. Instead, you’d want principles that protect everyone, especially if you might end up among those with the least advantages.
The original position works like a moral laboratory. By stripping away all the details about who you are, you’re forced to think about justice from an impartial point of view. It actually builds on the old social contract idea, but takes it a step further by focusing on fairness from the very beginning.
Now, imagine being in this position. You’re rational and reasonable—you want a good life, of course. But you also realize you could wind up anywhere in society’s hierarchy. That makes you lean toward rules that are fair for everyone, not just the lucky or the powerful.
The veil of ignorance is such a powerful tool for thinking about justice, because it pushes us toward empathy and impartiality. It’s like asking, “What if I had to step into anyone’s shoes? Would I still accept these rules?” This way, it cuts through the usual biases and self-interest that so often creep into real-world debates about justice.
By using the original position and the veil of ignorance, we get a solid foundation for justice as fairness. It gives us a way to test if the rules of our society really are legitimate—by asking, “Would people actually choose these principles if they didn’t know where they’d end up?”
That’s a pretty powerful check for fairness, don’t you think?
